steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Implementations section of an encyclopedia article on H.264/Advanced Video Coding: browser support and the HTML5 video codec debate, Cisco's OpenH264, and hardware versus software encoders.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- HTML5 video and browser support for H.264
- Firefox adding H.264
- Cisco OpenH264 and iOS
- Software encoders
- Hardware: software vs hardware trade-offs, CPU-based flexibility, Quick Sync, ASIC/FPGA, TI DSP

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- HTML5 debate
  - 2009: HTML5 working group split between Ogg Theora (free, thought unencumbered by patents) and H.264 (patented technology)
  - July 2009: Google and Apple said to support H.264, Mozilla and Opera Ogg Theora; eventually Google, Mozilla, Opera all supported Theora and WebM with VP8; Theora support removed 2023–2024
  - Microsoft: Internet Explorer 9 added HTML 5 video with H.264
  - Gartner Symposium/ITXpo, November 2010: Steve Ballmer on "HTML 5 or Silverlight?" — [quote: universal -> HTML5]
  - January 2011: Google pulling H.264 from Chrome, supporting Theora and WebM/VP8 to use only open formats
- Firefox
  - March 18, 2012: H.264 in Firefox on mobile; prevalence of H.264 video, power-efficiency of dedicated decoder hardware
  - February 20, 2013: decoding H.264 on Windows 7 and above, relies on Windows' built-in decoding libraries
  - Firefox 35.0, January 13, 2015: H.264 on OS X 10.6 and higher
- OpenH264
  - October 30, 2013: Rowan Trollope (Cisco Systems) — binaries and source of OpenH264 under Simplified BSD license; Cisco pays royalties to MPEG LA for projects using its precompiled binaries -> free to use
  - projects using source instead of binaries responsible for royalties
  - targets: x86 and ARM; Linux, Windows XP and later, Mac OS X, Android; not iOS (no fetching/installing binary modules from Internet)
  - same day: Brendan Eich (Mozilla) — Firefox to use Cisco's binaries where platform codecs unavailable
  - source code published December 9, 2013
  - iOS 8 (September 2014): Apple's Video Toolbox Framework gives direct access to hardware H.264/AVC encoding and decoding
- Software encoders (heading only)
- Hardware
  - encoding/decoding need lots of computation for specific arithmetic -> software on general-purpose CPUs less power-efficient
  - but 6- or 8-core consumer CPUs since around 2016, quad-core x86 as of January 2020, can do real-time SD and HD encoding
  - compression efficiency depends on algorithmic implementation, not hardware vs software -> difference is power efficiency, flexibility, cost
  - special-purpose hardware for power/size: full encode/decode or acceleration within CPU-controlled environment
  - CPU-based: more flexible, multiple formats/bit rates/resolutions (multi-screen video), container format support, advertising features; easier load balancing of concurrent sessions
  - Intel "Sandy Bridge" 2nd gen Core i3/i5/i7, January 2011 CES: on-chip full HD H.264 encoder, Intel Quick Sync Video
  - hardware encoder: ASIC or FPGA
  - ASIC core designs licensed from a few companies: Chips&Media, Allegro DVT, On2 (formerly Hantro, acquired by Google), Imagination Technologies, NGCodec; some offer both FPGA and ASIC
  - Texas Instruments ARM + DSP cores: DSP H.264 BP encoding 1080p at 30 fps; flexible codecs (optimized DSP code), more efficient than software on generic CPU

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 2009 the HTML5 working group was split between people supporting Ogg Theora, a free video format that is thought to be unencumbered by patents, and people supporting H.264, which contains patented technology. As late as July 2009, Google and Apple were said to support H.264, and Mozilla and Opera supported Ogg Theora (in the end Google, Mozilla and Opera all supported Theora and WebM with VP8, but Theora support was removed in 2023–2024). Microsoft added support for HTML 5 video encoded using H.264 with the release of Internet Explorer 9. At the Gartner Symposium/ITXpo in November 2010, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer was asked "HTML 5 or Silverlight?" and he answered "If you want to do something that is universal, there is no question the world is going HTML5." In January 2011 Google announced that they were pulling H.264 support from their Chrome browser, and would support both Theora and WebM/VP8 so as to use only open formats.

On March 18, 2012, Mozilla announced H.264 support in Firefox on mobile devices. This was because of how prevalent H.264-encoded video is and the increased power-efficiency of using the dedicated H.264 decoder hardware that is common on those devices. On February 20, 2013, Mozilla implemented support in Firefox for decoding H.264 on Windows 7 and above. This relies on the decoding libraries built into Windows. Firefox 35.0, which was released on January 13, 2015, supports H.264 on OS X 10.6 and higher.

On October 30, 2013, Rowan Trollope from Cisco Systems announced that Cisco would release both binaries and source code of an H.264 video codec called OpenH264 under the Simplified BSD license. Cisco would also pay all royalties for its use to MPEG LA for any software projects that use Cisco's precompiled binaries, which makes Cisco's OpenH264 binaries free to use. But software projects that use Cisco's source code instead of the binaries would be legally responsible for paying all the royalties to MPEG LA. The target CPU architectures include x86 and ARM, and the target operating systems include Linux, Windows XP and later, Mac OS X, and Android. iOS was notably not on this list, because it does not allow applications to fetch and install binary modules from the Internet. Also on October 30, 2013, Brendan Eich from Mozilla wrote that Mozilla would use Cisco's binaries in future versions of Firefox to add H.264 support to Firefox where platform codecs are not available. Cisco published the OpenH264 source code on December 9, 2013.

- iOS 8 (September 2014): Apple Video Toolbox Framework, direct access to hardware H.264/AVC encoding and decoding

### Software encoders

### Hardware

- heavy computation -> software on general-purpose CPUs less power-efficient; but 6/8-core consumer CPUs since around 2016, quad-core x86 as of January 2020 do real-time SD and HD encoding
- compression efficiency depends on algorithm, not hardware vs software -> power efficiency, flexibility, cost
- special-purpose hardware: full encode/decode or acceleration within CPU-controlled environment
- CPU-based more flexible: multiple formats, bit rates, resolutions (multi-screen video), container format support, advertising features; easier load balancing
- Intel "Sandy Bridge" Core i3/i5/i7, January 2011 CES -> Intel Quick Sync Video
- ASIC or FPGA; ASIC cores licensed from Chips&Media, Allegro DVT, On2 (formerly Hantro, acquired by Google), Imagination Technologies, NGCodec
- Texas Instruments ARM + DSP: H.264 BP 1080p at 30 fps; flexible, more efficient than generic CPU

steps.text:
In 2009 the HTML5 working group was split between people supporting Ogg Theora, a free video format that is thought to be unencumbered by patents, and people supporting H.264, which contains patented technology. As late as July 2009, Google and Apple were said to support H.264, and Mozilla and Opera supported Ogg Theora (in the end Google, Mozilla and Opera all supported Theora and WebM with VP8, but Theora support was removed in 2023–2024). Microsoft added support for HTML 5 video encoded using H.264 with the release of Internet Explorer 9. At the Gartner Symposium/ITXpo in November 2010, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer was asked "HTML 5 or Silverlight?" and he answered "If you want to do something that is universal, there is no question the world is going HTML5." In January 2011 Google announced that they were pulling H.264 support from their Chrome browser, and would support both Theora and WebM/VP8 so as to use only open formats.

On March 18, 2012, Mozilla announced H.264 support in Firefox on mobile devices. This was because of how prevalent H.264-encoded video is and the increased power-efficiency of using the dedicated H.264 decoder hardware that is common on those devices. On February 20, 2013, Mozilla implemented support in Firefox for decoding H.264 on Windows 7 and above. This relies on the decoding libraries built into Windows. Firefox 35.0, which was released on January 13, 2015, supports H.264 on OS X 10.6 and higher.

On October 30, 2013, Rowan Trollope from Cisco Systems announced that Cisco would release both binaries and source code of an H.264 video codec called OpenH264 under the Simplified BSD license. Cisco would also pay all royalties for its use to MPEG LA for any software projects that use Cisco's precompiled binaries, which makes Cisco's OpenH264 binaries free to use. But software projects that use Cisco's source code instead of the binaries would be legally responsible for paying all the royalties to MPEG LA. The target CPU architectures include x86 and ARM, and the target operating systems include Linux, Windows XP and later, Mac OS X, and Android. iOS was notably not on this list, because it does not allow applications to fetch and install binary modules from the Internet. Also on October 30, 2013, Brendan Eich from Mozilla wrote that Mozilla would use Cisco's binaries in future versions of Firefox to add H.264 support to Firefox where platform codecs are not available. Cisco published the OpenH264 source code on December 9, 2013.

iOS was not supported by the 2013 Cisco software release, but Apple updated its Video Toolbox Framework with iOS 8 (released in September 2014) so that it provides direct access to hardware-based H.264/AVC video encoding and decoding.

### Software encoders

### Hardware

H.264 encoding and decoding need a lot of computational power for specific arithmetic operations, so software implementations that run on general-purpose CPUs are usually less power-efficient. However consumer-grade CPUs with 6 or 8 cores since around 2016, and quad-core general-purpose x86 CPUs as of January 2020, have enough computational power to do real-time SD and HD encoding. Compression efficiency depends on the video algorithmic implementations and not on whether a hardware or software implementation is used. So the difference between hardware-based and software-based implementations is more about power efficiency, flexibility and cost. Special-purpose hardware may be used to improve power efficiency and reduce size, either for the whole encoding or decoding process, or for acceleration assistance inside a CPU-controlled environment.

CPU-based solutions are known to be much more flexible, especially when the encoding has to be done concurrently in multiple formats, multiple bit rates and resolutions (multi-screen video), and maybe with extra features such as container format support, advanced integrated advertising features, etc. CPU-based software solutions also generally make it a lot easier to load balance multiple concurrent encoding sessions inside the same CPU.

The 2nd generation Intel "Sandy Bridge" Core i3/i5/i7 processors, which were introduced at the January 2011 CES (Consumer Electronics Show), offer an on-chip hardware full HD H.264 encoder that is known as Intel Quick Sync Video.

A hardware H.264 encoder can be either an ASIC or an FPGA.

ASIC encoders with H.264 encoder functionality are available from many different semiconductor companies, but the core design that is used in the ASIC is usually licensed from one of a few companies such as Chips&Media, Allegro DVT, On2 (formerly Hantro, acquired by Google), Imagination Technologies, NGCodec. Some companies offer both FPGA and ASIC products.

Texas Instruments makes a line of ARM + DSP cores that do DSP H.264 BP encoding 1080p at 30 fps. This gives flexibility with respect to codecs (which are implemented as highly optimized DSP code) while being more efficient than software on a generic CPU.
